issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly describes the study as using a national probability/general population/nationally representative sample, but the Methods clearly state participants were recruited from an introductory psychology participant pool and were predominantly young students. This contradiction affects interpretation, external validity, and the paper's central framing.
issues.quote: Abstract: "We examine the longitudinal influence of SDO and RWA on people’s willingness to change their behaviour to benefit the environment in a national probability sample over five years." ... Method: "We recruited participants through the introductory psychology participant pool at Victoria University of Wellington."

issues.description: The manuscript makes strong claims of national representativeness and general population inference, but the described sample is a convenience sample of mostly 19-year-old psychology participants, 68% female, 86% Pākehā. Results cannot be generalized to the New Zealand population, much less used to contrast with student samples as if this were non-student general-population data.
issues.quote: "We expand on Stanley et al.’s study by using a large, national probability sample spanning five years..."; "Of the 374 participants included in this study, the average age was 19 years at Time 1 ... and 68% were female ... the majority (86%) identified as Pākehā"; "Our research uses a nationally representative sample, meaning that our results are highly generalisable"

issues.description: The paper claims to study willingness to change behavior / willingness to sacrifice for the environment, but the Measures section defines environmentalism as concern about environmental problems using only two concern/exaggeration items. Concern is not equivalent to willingness to sacrifice behaviorally. This mismatch undermines construct validity and interpretation of findings.
issues.quote: Abstract: "people’s willingness to change their behaviour to benefit the environment" ... Methods: "Environmentalism was measured as participants’ concern about environmental problems. These items were modelled from Liu and Sibley’s [28] environmental concern scale, 'How concerned are you about the current state of the natural environment?' and 'To what extent do you think environmental problems have been exaggerated?'"

issues.description: The manuscript alternates between describing the dependent variable as environmental concern, willingness to change behavior, willingness to sacrifice, and willingness to make sacrifices for the environment. These are distinct constructs. The inconsistency makes it unclear what was actually analyzed and reported.
issues.quote: "We used path analysis to examine associations between SDO, RWA and willingness to sacrifice for the environment."; "Environmentalism was measured as participants’ concern about environmental problems."; Table 1 labels outcome as "WILL = willingness to make sacrifices for the environment."

issues.description: The paper omits essential details about wave-specific sample sizes, attrition across five waves, inclusion criteria for the analytic sample, and whether the 374 participants completed all waves or were partially observed. Referring readers to a website is insufficient for evaluating bias and replicability.
issues.quote: "This study uses data from individuals who participated across five semesters of the project (from 2009 to 2013)."; "Full details about the sample, including the procedure, retention, and demographics of participants, are available on the NZAVS website."

issues.description: Using listwise deletion in a five-wave longitudinal model can substantially reduce effective sample size and bias estimates unless missingness is MCAR. No justification, missing-data diagnostics, or comparison with FIML/multiple imputation is provided.
issues.quote: "Analyses were conducted using listwise deletion."

issues.subcategory: unaddressed omitted item at one wave
issues.description: One RWA item was not assessed at time two, but the manuscript does not explain how this planned missingness was handled in scale construction or longitudinal modeling, nor whether measurement comparability was preserved.
issues.quote: "The item 'Some of the best people in our country are those who are challenging our government, criticizing religion, and ignoring the “normal way” things are supposed to be done', was not assessed at time two, but included in all other time points."

issues.description: The study makes longitudinal comparisons and imposes stationarity, yet does not report any tests of longitudinal measurement invariance for SDO, RWA, or environmentalism. Without demonstrating at least metric/scalar invariance, cross-time paths may reflect changing measurement properties rather than change in constructs.
issues.quote: "We tested the reciprocal influences between the constructs with a stationary cross-lagged model where all parameters are set as time-invariant."

issues.description: The authors constrain cross-lagged effects to be equal across all intervals because they are interested in overall effects, but provide no substantive or empirical justification that effects should be stationary over five years. This may mask heterogeneity across intervals and distort estimates.
issues.quote: "We imposed this stationary cross-lagged model because we were more interested in the overall and comparative effects of SDO and RWA on changes in environmentalism, and not on whether these effects change during the interval measured."

issues.description: The manuscript does not adequately specify whether analyses used latent variables or observed scores, how items were modeled, whether correlated residuals across constructs within waves were included, whether autoregressive residuals were allowed, what estimator was used, and how standard errors/CIs were computed. Replication and evaluation are therefore limited.
issues.quote: "The model included three variables across five measurement points and was conducted in Mplus... A copy of the Mplus syntax used will be available on the NZAVS website upon acceptance of the manuscript."

issues.description: Regression results report "B" followed by "SD" rather than standard error, implying confusion between standard deviation and standard error. If these values are SEs, they are mislabeled; if SDs, the inferential statistics are uninterpretable.
issues.quote: "SDO was a stronger predictor of change in environmental sacrifice (B = -.11, SD = .01, p < .001...) than RWA (B = -.02, SD = .01, p = .001...)"

issues.description: Several chi-square difference/Wald test statistics are reported incorrectly as "2(1)" instead of χ²(1), suggesting reporting errors. This is not merely typographical because these tests are central to claims of directional differences.
issues.quote: "We found that our original model provides comparable fit to the data 2(1) = 2.34, p = .126"; "the lagged effect on SDO was stronger than the reverse (2(1) = 39.97, p < .001)"

issues.subcategory: contradictory inference from nonsignificant model comparison
issues.description: The authors conclude SDO is a stronger predictor than RWA despite reporting that constraining the two paths to equality did not significantly worsen fit (p = .126). This is an inferential error: the reported comparison does not support a significant difference between predictors.
issues.quote: "We found that our original model provides comparable fit to the data 2(1) = 2.34, p = .126, but based on the pattern of unstandardized coefficients we interpret SDO as a stronger predictor"

issues.subcategory: claim of significant stronger predictor inconsistent with test
issues.description: The Discussion states that SDO is a significantly stronger prospective predictor than RWA, but the Results explicitly report a nonsignificant equality-constraint comparison. This contradiction affects the paper's main conclusion.
issues.quote: Results: "2(1) = 2.34, p = .126" ... Discussion: "In this context, both SDO and RWA are related to environmentalism, but SDO is a significantly stronger prospective predictor than RWA."

issues.description: The reported chi-square difference of 15,389.13 for comparing two tiny cross-lagged coefficients in a sample of 374 is implausibly large and strongly suggests a reporting or computational error. Such an extreme value undermines confidence in the statistical reporting.
issues.quote: "These lagged effects were also statistically different (2(1) = 15,389.13, p < .001)"

issues.description: Key results are said to be shown in Figure 1, but the manuscript text does not provide the full set of autoregressive and cross-lagged coefficients, confidence intervals, or standardized estimates. Because the figure is not fully reproduced, the core model cannot be independently evaluated from the manuscript text.
issues.quote: "Figure 1. Unstandardized parameters assessing the association between SDO, RWA, and willingness to sacrifice for the environment (WILL)."

issues.subcategory: accepting poor fit despite inadequate comparative fit index
issues.description: The authors accept the model despite CFI = .86, which is commonly interpreted as below acceptable thresholds for good fit. Their rationale that some indices are less affected by complexity is too weak without sensitivity analyses or alternative models.
issues.quote: "Overall, model fit was poorer for those indices affected by model complexity (e.g. χ2(2279) = 36511.73, p < .001, CFI = .86), however those less influenced by complexity pointed to good fit ... therefore the model was accepted."

issues.description: The manuscript provides little information about alternative model specifications considered, whether unconstrained models were tested before imposing stationarity, or whether correlated residual structures and other decisions were chosen post hoc. This raises concerns about analytic flexibility.
issues.quote: "We started by constraining the cross-lagged associations between the constructs to be the same in each measurement point... We imposed this stationary cross-lagged model because we were more interested in the overall and comparative effects"

issues.description: Given the complex longitudinal SEM and multiple possible modeling decisions, the absence of any preregistration or a priori analysis plan raises concern about researcher degrees of freedom. This is especially relevant because the paper makes strong directional claims from a flexible modeling framework.
issues.quote: No preregistration, registered analysis plan, or prior specification of model constraints is reported anywhere in the manuscript.

issues.subcategory: causal language from observational cross-lagged model
issues.description: The paper repeatedly treats cross-lagged associations as establishing causal pathways (e.g., ideology causes environmentalism, desire to dominate leads to lower environmentalism). Standard cross-lagged panel models with observational survey data do not establish causality absent stronger assumptions and controls.
issues.quote: "These results suggest that there is a causal pathway from ideological attitudes to environmentalism."; "This result indicates that the desire to dominate leads to lower environmentalism in the future"

issues.subcategory: cross-lagged model claimed to disentangle directionality
issues.description: The Results state that the analyses "help us disentangle the directionality" of relationships. Cross-lagged associations may be consistent with temporal ordering but do not by themselves disentangle directionality from stable trait confounds, measurement error, or omitted variables, especially in a traditional CLPM.
issues.quote: "These analyses help us disentangle the directionality of the relationships"

issues.description: Although the Discussion briefly mentions possible third variables, the model includes no covariates or controls for plausible confounders such as political ideology, socioeconomic status, education, personality/worldviews, or period effects. Therefore directional interpretations are highly vulnerable to omitted-variable bias.
issues.quote: "a possible alternative explanation is that the relationship between ideology and environmentalism across time is explained by a third variable... Future research could test these and other alternative explanations"

issues.description: SDO, RWA, and environmental attitudes are all highly stable trait-like constructs. A traditional cross-lagged panel model conflates between-person stability with within-person change and can produce misleading cross-lagged effects. A random-intercept CLPM or latent trait-state approach would be more appropriate.
issues.quote: "As shown in Figure 1, across all time points, SDO, RWA, and willingness to sacrifice were all relatively stable over time"; "We tested the reciprocal influences between the constructs with a stationary cross-lagged model"

issues.description: Environmentalism is operationalized with only two items, one of which concerns exaggeration of environmental problems. This narrow operationalization may capture skepticism/concern rather than willingness to sacrifice or broad environmentalism, limiting validity and breadth of inference.
issues.quote: "Environmentalism was measured as participants’ concern about environmental problems... 'How concerned are you about the current state of the natural environment?' and 'To what extent do you think environmental problems have been exaggerated?'"

issues.subcategory: shortened ideology scales with low reliability
issues.description: The study uses abridged 6-item versions of SDO and RWA and acknowledges poorer reliability than full scales. Low reliability attenuates effects, complicates longitudinal inference, and may differentially bias comparisons between SDO and RWA if reliability differs across constructs or waves.
issues.quote: "Reliabilities for SDO and RWA were poorer than is typically the case when the full scales are used"

issues.description: Only Time 1 reliabilities are shown; no wave-by-wave reliability estimates or longitudinal measurement properties are reported. This is particularly important because one RWA item is missing at time 2 and the scales are shortened.
issues.quote: "Table 1 presents the descriptive statistics and correlations between our variables at Time 1. Reliabilities for SDO and RWA were poorer..."

issues.description: The manuscript calls the design a five-year analysis and says data span 2009 to 2013, but also says participants took part across five semesters. Five semesters is not equivalent to five annual waves and introduces ambiguity about the spacing of measurements.
issues.quote: Title: "A five-year cross-lagged analysis"; Method: "participated across five semesters of the project (from 2009 to 2013)"

issues.description: The exact timing of the five measurement occasions is not reported. Cross-lag interpretation depends on lag length; annual versus semesterly intervals imply very different processes.
issues.quote: "across five semesters of the project (from 2009 to 2013)"

issues.subcategory: no discussion of panel conditioning/cohort effects
issues.description: Repeated measurement over multiple years can be influenced by panel conditioning, historical events, or cohort maturation, especially in a young student sample. The manuscript does not consider these design threats despite making temporal claims.
issues.quote: No mention is made of historical period effects, maturation, or panel conditioning in the five-wave design.

issues.description: The manuscript states that social dominance theory proposes that SDO and RWA are separate but interrelated and together predict attitudes. This formulation more closely resembles Duckitt's dual-process model than Sidanius and Pratto's theory, risking theoretical confusion.
issues.quote: "Sidanius and Pratto’s [1] social dominance theory proposes that SDO and RWA are separate but interrelated, and together predict attitudes towards different social groups."

issues.description: The Discussion infers that the motivation to exploit the environment comes from desire for dominance and submission to authority, but the study does not measure motives, dominance over nature, anthropocentrism, or authority submission mechanisms. The conclusion overreaches beyond observed associations.
issues.quote: "The motivation to exploit the environment comes primarily from the desire for dominance, and to a lesser extent from the desire to submit to authority."

issues.subcategory: operationalization does not match climate-change claims
issues.description: The paper frames the topic as climate change denial and willingness to act on climate change, but the actual environmentalism measure concerns general environmental concern/exaggeration. Conclusions about climate change mitigation are therefore not directly supported by the measurement used here.
issues.quote: Abstract: "less willingness to act on climate change"; Methods: environmentalism items are "current state of the natural environment" and whether "environmental problems have been exaggerated"

issues.subcategory: unsupported claim from non-overlapping confidence intervals
issues.description: The authors infer a stronger zero-order correlation because confidence intervals do not overlap. Comparing overlap of separate CIs is not the proper statistical test for the difference between dependent correlations sharing a variable.
issues.quote: "the zero-order correlation between SDO and environmentalism was stronger than the correlation for RWA, as indicated by the non-overlapping confidence interval."

issues.description: The manuscript states CIs are based on 1000 iterations for descriptive statistics and correlations but does not explain the resampling method, whether it accounted for dependency, or why bootstrapping was used here. This obscures interpretation of Table 1.
issues.quote: "Numbers in square brackets represent 95% confidence intervals based on 1000 iterations."

issues.description: The Methods mention constraining residual variance for the same item over time, implying item-level measurement modeling, but elsewhere the model is described simply as three variables across five time points. It is unclear whether the analysis was at the item level or scale level, which matters for model meaning.
issues.quote: "We also constrained to equality the residual variance for the same item over time, so item 1 in the SDO scale had equal residual variance across all time points."

issues.description: The description of model constraints repeats the same statement about constraining cross-lagged associations to equality, suggesting possible editing errors and making the model specification hard to follow.
issues.quote: "We started by constraining the cross-lagged associations between the constructs to be the same in each measurement point... Finally, we constrained the cross-lagged associations between the constructs to be the same in each measurement point."

issues.description: Cross-lagged panel models require specification of within-wave covariances among constructs and often residual covariances; none are reported. Without this information, readers cannot assess whether the lagged paths are conditioned on contemporaneous associations appropriately.
issues.quote: The manuscript does not report within-wave covariances/residual correlations among SDO, RWA, and environmentalism in the panel model.

issues.subcategory: sample demographic narrowness unacknowledged in main claims
issues.description: The sample is overwhelmingly young, female, and Pākehā, yet the main claims are phrased as if they apply broadly to 'people' and 'the general population'. Demographic narrowness could moderate ideology-environment relations and should materially temper conclusions.
issues.quote: "Of the 374 participants included in this study, the average age was 19 years ... 68% were female ... 86% identified as Pākehā"; "The take home message from our study is that for those in the general population..."

issues.subcategory: unknown effective N after listwise deletion
issues.description: Because listwise deletion was used, the effective sample size for the SEM may be substantially lower than 374 if any participant missed any wave/item. The manuscript never reports the actual N used in the main model.
issues.quote: "Of the 374 participants included in this study... Analyses were conducted using listwise deletion."

issues.subcategory: directional claims despite acknowledged reverse paths
issues.description: Even though the model reports significant reverse paths from environmentalism to ideology, the paper still concludes unidirectionally that desire to dominate leads to lower environmentalism. This selectively emphasizes one direction and understates reciprocal/ambiguous ordering.
issues.quote: "This result indicates that the desire to dominate leads to lower environmentalism in the future"; earlier: "The lagged effect of willingness to sacrifice on both SDO and RWA were statistically significant and negative"

issues.description: The claim that findings suggest New Zealanders are socialized into authoritarianism more than social dominance is not directly tested and goes far beyond the reported cross-lag coefficients. National socialization processes cannot be inferred from this sample or model.
issues.quote: "Because we found that RWA predicts SDO over time, but SDO does not predict RWA, this suggests that New Zealander’s are socialized into authoritarianism to a greater extent than social dominance."
